lessons.title: Why Great Strategies Quietly Die
lessons.key_idea: The biggest threat to any important goal is the whirlwind, the urgent daily work that consumes the time and energy needed for anything new.
issues: scene 7: The magnifying glass sits on top of the drowning-figure box. It covers the box's right edge and the water. Its handle ends right against the 'DROWNING IN URGENT WORK' label, so the group reads as cluttered and stacked. (fix: Move the magnifier to the right of the box, into the gap before the culprit pills, or shrink it. Keep at least 24px clearance from the box and the label.)

lessons.title: The Four Disciplines at a Glance
lessons.key_idea: Execution becomes reliable when teams practise four connected disciplines: focus, lead measures, a scoreboard, and regular accountability.

lessons.title: Focus on the Wildly Important
lessons.key_idea: Discipline 1 says the more goals you chase at once, the fewer you achieve, so pick one or two that truly matter most.

lessons.title: From X to Y by When
lessons.key_idea: A wildly important goal must be measurable and time-bound, written as moving from a starting line to a finish line by a deadline.

lessons.title: Lead Measures Beat Lag Measures
lessons.key_idea: Discipline 2 says to track the predictive actions you can influence, like daily calories and exercise, rather than only the end result, like weight lost.

lessons.title: Keep a Players' Scoreboard
lessons.key_idea: Discipline 3 says a simple, visible scoreboard showing whether the team is winning drives far more engagement than a complex report.

lessons.title: The Weekly Rhythm of Accountability
lessons.key_idea: Discipline 4 says short, regular team sessions, where people report on last week's commitments and make new ones, keep the goal alive.

lessons.title: Winning Inside the Whirlwind
lessons.key_idea: The four disciplines work together to protect a small slice of time for your top goal, so progress happens even while the whirlwind keeps blowing.

plan.title: The 4 Disciplines of Execution
plan.author: Chris McChesney, Sean Covey, and Jim Huling
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's core framework well, including the whirlwind, the four disciplines, lead and lag measures, scoreboards and weekly accountability sessions, though I am less certain of every case study's details.
plan.one_liner: Your daily whirlwind is quietly killing your biggest goals. Here are four disciplines to fight back.
plan.summary: Most leaders can set a strategy. Far fewer can get it done. This book argues that the real enemy of execution is not laziness or bad ideas but the whirlwind, the endless urgent work that keeps the day running and swallows everything new. To break through, the authors offer four disciplines. First, focus on one or two wildly important goals instead of many. Second, act on lead measures, the small actions you control that drive results, rather than obsessing over lagging outcomes. Third, keep a simple, compelling scoreboard so the team always knows whether it is winning. Fourth, create a cadence of accountability through short weekly meetings where everyone commits to specific actions. Together, these disciplines turn vague strategy into steady, visible progress, even while the whirlwind keeps blowing.
